title: Dhurandhar: Part 2
synopsis: Three years after Karachi, you live in Lonavala under a name that isn't yours. A man you killed once is, apparently, alive. The agency needs you back. Your wife of paper says no.

nodes.text: Mist coming down the hills like something poured. The kettle you bought three years ago with cash, in a shop where nobody wrote your name in a book. Rabia on the porch with a novel, on page nine and not turning it, which means she is thinking rather than reading. And the phone in the drawer beneath the tea towels — the dead phone, the one no living person has the number for — starts to ring.

choices.consequence: You cross the room in four steps you have not needed in three years. Your body remembers the walk before you decide to take it.
You count nineteen rings. Rabia does not look up from the page she is not reading. Then it starts again.

nodes.text: A woman's voice, unhurried, no name offered. She says Karachi never closed, which is a sentence with a file number standing behind it. She says Dubai, Thursday, and gives you a hotel that does not take walk-ins. She does not try to persuade you, which is its own technique. And halfway through you work out why they woke you specifically: everyone else who ever saw your first handler's face is dead.

choices.text: Agree to a meeting in Mumbai
choices.consequence: You give her a public place and a daylight hour. It is the last condition in this whole thing you will get to set.
You say no and put the phone back in the drawer. It does not ring again, which is how you learn they have gone around you.

nodes.text: She sees the phone before you have it out of the drawer. She sees your shoulders drop half an inch, which is a thing only she can read. She marks her page properly, with the ribbon, and sets the book on the arm of the chair. You promised me, she says, without heat. I know, you say. The mist keeps coming down. The morning has aged twenty years since the kettle boiled.

choices.consequence: You say the word no out loud, to her face, and in that moment you mean it completely. She knows you mean it. She also knows what that is worth.

choices.text: Tell her you need to hear them out
choices.consequence: You ask for one meeting and one hour, and she agrees the way people agree to a diagnosis rather than to a plan.

nodes.text: An Irani cafe off Colaba, two ceiling fans, bun maska nobody touches. Your new handler is forty-odd, sharp, and frightened in a way she is managing very well. The dossier crosses the marble inside a bakery bag. Third page: a ledger of payments out of a bank in Sharjah, and on the receiving side, spelled correctly, the name of the cover wife you buried an entire life underneath.

choices.consequence: You leave the bag on the table and the money under the saucer. You get four streets before you understand you have already been briefed.
You ask for all of it, which is how they take you, because all of it is a thing you cannot afterwards un-know.

nodes.text: Khala Bhabhi's voice out of Karachi at one in the morning, on a number you have given to nobody. She is older and drier and she does not waste the first sentence on greetings. He is alive, she says. And he has your wife's name. Not the cover wife. Rabia — the woman asleep in the next room, in a house that four services are supposed to be unable to find.

choices.consequence: You wake her at two and she is dressed and packed in nine minutes without asking a single question. That is not comforting.
You spend a day verifying and let her sleep through it. You will never settle whether that was steadiness or cowardice.

nodes.text: You land on a passport with three stamps in it, all of them boring. The hotel room is on the ninth floor with a door that closes properly and a window that does not open. The brief is one sentence wide: establish whether the man who walked out of the Karachi house three years ago is the man you shot. You have forty-eight hours before they send somebody who does it louder.

choices.text: Take the mission and run it carefully
choices.consequence: You run it their way — patterns, distance, no contact. Careful is slower, and slow is a thing you can no longer afford at home.

choices.text: Run a counter-op of your own
choices.consequence: You accept the brief in writing and open a second operation the same evening that nobody has authorised, including you.

nodes.text: Two hills over, a house with a tin roof and a kilometre of visible road in both directions. Rabia unpacks without being told where anything goes. She checks the back door, then the window latches, then the sightlines from the kitchen, in that order — the correct order. She is furious with you and she is extremely good at this, and it occurs to you that you have never once asked where she learned it.

choices.text: Take her with you to Dubai
choices.consequence: She travels as your wife, which she is, on paper that for once is not a lie. It is the first time you have not had to invent her.
You go without her and she does not argue, which frightens you considerably more than the argument would have.

nodes.text: Noon, a gym on Sheikh Zayed Road, treadmills facing the glass. He is on the second one — greyer, forty pounds lighter, alive. He sees you in the reflection before you have finished looking at him. He does not run. He finishes his water, walks out to the car park with both hands loose and open at his sides, stops six feet away, and tells you he has been wanting to apologise.

choices.consequence: You stand in a car park in forty-two degrees and let a dead man talk for an hour. Every minute of it is unauthorised.
You put him in the boot of a rented sedan, which is procedure, and which means the men who own him now know exactly where he stopped.

nodes.text: You build it out of people no ledger will ever admit to. Khala Bhabhi in Karachi with forty years of grocers and cousins. A Malayali stringer in Deira who will photograph anything for cash. Your first handler, who is supposed to be in a grave in Pune and is not. And Rabia at a whiteboard in a Lonavala kitchen, because she turns out to be the best analyst any of you have ever worked with.

choices.text: Run it as a private circle
choices.consequence: Nothing on paper, nothing on a state server, nobody to sign off. You have never been this exposed, or this fast.

choices.text: Use it to clean your name with the agency
choices.consequence: You feed them just enough to become useful again, which is the same as handing your leash back across the table.

nodes.text: He talks for two hours and never once asks you for anything. He was run for fourteen months by a third service — not Pakistan, not you, a country whose embassy sends you a card at Diwali. He has wanted out since the second month. There is a hard drive taped inside the frame of a bathroom mirror in a flat in Karama. He kept it, he says, in case somebody like you ever came.

choices.consequence: You decide in a car park, on instinct, against every rule you have ever taught. You are right, and you would not have survived being wrong.
You take four days to check the drive against three sources. He waits in the flat and does not run, which is evidence of a kind.

nodes.text: Your stringer buys a server log off a sysadmin for the price of a motorcycle. The Karachi operation three years ago was not run out of Rawalpindi at all. It was routed through a friendly capital, through a service that shares your threat assessments and drinks at your embassy receptions. The betrayal is not personal, which somehow makes it worse. Your own agency has been lied to exactly as thoroughly as you were.

choices.text: Take the evidence to the agency
choices.consequence: You take it in the front door, which is loyal, and which means eight men now get to decide what happens to your family.

choices.text: Take it to a journalist for outside pressure
choices.consequence: You choose a woman in Delhi who has been sued four times and lost nothing. Once it is printed, nobody can quietly mislay it.

nodes.text: Dubai, week three, a handover in a mall car park that goes wrong in the ordinary way. She reads it two seconds before you do and moves the meeting point by text without consulting anybody. Afterwards you sit in the car with the engine off and understand she is not learning this. She has been carrying it the whole time you were teaching her to make chai for men who might have killed you.

choices.consequence: You put her name on the operational file. It gets her cleared, insured, and permanently on a list in three countries.

choices.text: Keep her work informal — protect her record
choices.consequence: You keep her off every page. It keeps her clean, and it means nothing she does will ever officially have happened.

nodes.text: She draws it on the back of a calendar: six months, three cities, four planted stories and one deliberately imperfect forgery the third country will be forced to publicly disown. She is sixty-eight. She has been running couriers since before you were commissioned. She says she has been waiting a long time for someone with your particular file to walk back through her door, and then she asks whether you want more tea.

choices.consequence: You give her half a year and both hands. It means missing the monsoon in Lonavala, and Rabia hears the missing before you say it.
You commit to six weeks and a review, which is honest, and which Khala Bhabhi accepts with a look that says she will get the rest regardless.

nodes.text: Six months. Two ambassadors recalled, three officers burned, one broadsheet forced into a correction that runs nine hundred words. The network comes apart in public, in the right order, on the right days. And nearly all of it was assembled at a kitchen table in Lonavala by a woman with a whiteboard and a man who is officially retired, over an internet connection that drops whenever it rains.

choices.text: Stay in the work, on your terms
choices.consequence: You take a consultancy on a contract you actually read, and the quiet power of being able to say no in writing.
You close the accounts, burn the passports, take the pension. The silence afterwards is very loud for about four months.

nodes.text: You come back to a house that has grown a smell of damp and a cat. The cat belongs to nobody and has decided, in your absence, that the porch is hers. On the mat there is a postcard from Lisbon with a painting on it — his own, badly photographed and worse painted. Tariq has taken up oils. Rabia laughs until she has to put the tea down on the step.

choices.text: Take Tariq's offer to visit Lisbon
choices.consequence: You write yes on the back of a bus ticket and post it. It is the least tradecraft you have managed in twenty years.

choices.text: Stay in Lonavala for the season
choices.consequence: You stay through the rains and repair the roof yourself, badly. It is the first thing you have built that nobody has to deny.

nodes.text: Spring, a fourth-floor flat in Graca with the windows open and washing strung on the line below. The paintings are genuinely terrible — you say so out loud and he agrees, delighted. He cooks bacalhau, gets it wrong, and serves it anyway. Somewhere between the second glass and the plates you register that you have not been a guest in a friend's home since you were twenty-six years old.

choices.consequence: You extend the ticket twice, then stop extending it and simply stay. Rabia arrives in June with two bags and no return date.
You go home in April with a bad painting rolled in a tube and hang it in the kitchen, where it wins every argument by being there.

nodes.text: You dig a bed four metres by two behind the house, and Rabia argues for tomatoes over chillies and wins on the evidence. None of it is symbolic. It is soil, a fence against the monkeys, and a running disagreement about water. The neighbours know you as the couple in the blue house. They do not know your name, either of your names. They bring you seedlings anyway.

choices.text: Keep the garden small and yours
choices.consequence: You decide four metres by two is the correct size for the rest of a life. Nobody else gets a key to the gate.

choices.text: Invite a young handler to learn
choices.consequence: You write one line to an old address: send me the next one you are about to waste. Somebody, eventually, replies.

nodes.text: A year split three ways — Lisbon in spring, Istanbul in autumn because Rabia wanted the bookshops, Lonavala for the rains. You learn to stand in a ferry queue without counting exits. You buy a guidebook, are embarrassed by it, and use it anyway. It takes most of a year to notice that these are countries you have only ever entered before, and never once lived in.

choices.text: Make Lisbon a real home half the year
choices.consequence: You sign a lease with your own name on it, in ink, at a desk. The strangeness of that lasts about a week.
You give up the flat and carry the last of it back to Lonavala. Two homes was one more than you could keep secure.

nodes.text: You write it in longhand, because a hard drive is a liability and a habit is a habit. Four hundred pages nobody will read: the first handler, the first lie, the specific weight of a boy in Karachi. Rabia edits in pencil and shows no mercy. Tariq sends a chapter of his own attempt in Portuguese, which you cannot read and keep regardless. Mostly it is an act of paying attention.

choices.consequence: You burn it in the garden bed in a steel bucket while Rabia watches. Writing it was the point. Keeping it never was.

choices.text: Lock it in a vault for fifty years
choices.consequence: You put it in a Bombay bank with instructions for 2076. Somebody not yet born gets to decide whether any of it mattered.

nodes.text: Two cups going cold on the porch rail because you have both been talking instead of drinking. The rain is late this year. She lists the options the way she lists anything, like an operations board: the garden and nothing beyond it, two kitchens on two continents, or the young woman the agency keeps offering to send, who would learn more in a month here than in five years anywhere else.

choices.text: Keep the porch and nothing else
choices.consequence: You choose the four metres by two, the cat, and the same walk every morning. It is a smaller life, and you have earned smaller.
You write the letter that afternoon and post it from the town so the postmark is not the house. She replies in six days.
You book two sets of flights for the next three years, which is either optimism or logistics, and at your age those have started to be the same thing.

nodes.text: Lonavala, all twelve months, with Rabia and a cat who has never once acknowledged being fed. You learn every neighbour's name and which of them lies about cricket scores. You walk the same loop each morning past the same three dogs. You sleep through the night. Against every line in a file that four services still keep and none of them will ever close, you have managed the impossible thing. You retired.

She arrives for tea in the wrong shoes and does not touch her cup for the first hour. You teach her the boring parts: how to be forgettable, how to write nothing down, how to keep the person at the other end of it alive. She comes back the next month, and the one after that. At sixty-three you become what your first handler was supposed to be — patient, unglamorous, and quietly devastating.

Half the year Lisbon, half the year Lonavala. Two bakers who know your order, two postmen, two entirely different ways of standing in a queue. Rabia keeps a garden in both and complains about Portuguese soil in Marathi. On a tram in April you finally work out what all that training was actually for: you can hold a whole environment in your head at once, and now you use it to notice a Tuesday.
